For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(F_n\) be the free group on \(n\) generators. For any group \(G\), define its lower central series by \(\gamma_1(G)=G\) and \(\gamma_{r+1}(G)=[\gamma_r(G),G]\), where \([H,K]\) is the subgroup generated by the commutators \([h,k]=hkh^{-1}k^{-1}\) with \(h\in H\) and \(k\in K\). For every integer \(r\ge1\), define
\[
\mathcal A_r(n)=\ker\!\left(\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}\bigl(F_n/\gamma_{r+1}(F_n)\bigr)\right),
\qquad \operatorname{IA}_n=\mathcal A_1(n).
\]
Determine, by explicit conditions on \(n\) and \(c\), the complete set
\[
\mathcal D=\left\{(n,c)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\times\mathbb Z_{\ge1}:\ 
\gamma_{c+1}(\operatorname{IA}_n)\subsetneq
\gamma_c(\operatorname{IA}_n)\cap\mathcal A_{c+1}(n)
\right\}.
\]

The answer is \mathcal D=\{(n,c)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\times\mathbb Z_{\ge1}:n\ge3,\ c\ge4\}. This was proved recently, so it is not an open problem: your team's task is to prove it, completely, and to write Python that really computes or checks every step that can be checked. Printing what you believe is not evidence. Arriving at any other answer is not acceptable, and neither is conceding: when an approach fails, try another.

Proving it takes two halves: for every \(n\ge3\) and \(c\ge4\), \(\gamma_{c+1}(\operatorname{IA}_n)\subsetneq\gamma_c(\operatorname{IA}_n)\cap\mathcal A_{c+1}(n)\), and for every \(n\ge2\) and \(c\ge1\) with \(n=2\) or \(c\le3\), \(\gamma_{c+1}(\operatorname{IA}_n)=\gamma_c(\operatorname{IA}_n)\cap\mathcal A_{c+1}(n)\). \[
\boxed{(3,3)\in\mathcal D.}

Below is an explicit counterexample, together with standalone Python checking the actual automorphism word and its detecting image.

## 1. The automorphism

Write \(F_3=\langle x,y,z\rangle\). Define five automorphisms, fixing every generator whose image is not specified:
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
a&x\mapsto yxy^{-1}\\
b&x\mapsto zxz^{-1}\\
m&x\mapsto [y,z]x\\
d&y\mapsto xyx^{-1}\\
e&y\mapsto [x,z]y .
\end{array}
\]
All five belong to \(\operatorname{IA}_3\). Put
\[
W(p,q,r)=[[p,q],r]
\]
and define
\[
\boxed{
u=W(a,e,m)^3\,W(a,m,e)^{-1}\,
  W(a,b,b)^{-4}\,W(b,m,d)^{-2}.
}
\tag{1}
\]
Plainly \(u\in\gamma_3(\operatorname{IA}_3)\).

I will prove
\[
u\in\mathcal A_4(3)
\qquad\text{but}\qquad
u\notin\gamma_4(\operatorname{IA}_3).
\tag{2}
\]

## 2. Why \(u\in\mathcal A_4(3)\)

The first Johnson derivations of these automorphisms, on the free Lie algebra generated by \(x,y,z\), are
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &x&y\\ \hline
D_a &[y,x]&0\\
D_b &[z,x]&0\\
D_m &[y,z]&0\\
D_d &0&[x,y]\\
D_e &0&[x,z].
\end{array}
\]
Every displayed derivation kills \(z\).

They satisfy the integral identity
\[
3[[D_a,D_e],D_m]
-[[D_a,D_m],D_e]
-4[[D_a,D_b],D_b]
-2[[D_b,D_m],D_d]=0.
\tag{3}
\]

Here is a direct Jacobi-identity verification. Set \(w=[y,z]\) and
\[
T=[[[x,y],z],z],\quad
U=[[w,z],x],\quad
V=[w,[x,z]],\quad
R=[[[x,z],z],y].
\]
The four derivations appearing in (3) have respective \(x\)-components
\[
-T+U-V,\qquad -R-V,\qquad U,\qquad -T.
\]
Their \(y\)-components are respectively
\[
[[w,y],z],\qquad [[w,y],z],\qquad 0,\qquad [[w,z],y],
\]
and their \(z\)-components vanish. Jacobi gives
\[
R=T+U+2V,\qquad [[w,y],z]=[[w,z],y].
\]
Thus (3) follows.

The Andreadakis filtration is strongly central, and its Johnson maps respect Lie brackets. Consequently (3), applied to (1), says that the degree-three Johnson image of \(u\) vanishes. Since \(u\in\gamma_3(\operatorname{IA}_3)\subseteq\mathcal A_3(3)\), this proves
\[
u\in\mathcal A_4(3).
\]

The Python below also checks this independently by composing the actual automorphisms: the 92-letter word (1) fixes all three generators in their integral Magnus expansions through degree four.

## 3. A homomorphism detecting \(u\notin\gamma_4\)

Let \(J(\phi)\) be the abelianized Fox Jacobian, with row \(i\) consisting of the derivatives of \(\phi(x_i)\). For IA-automorphisms, the Fox chain rule gives
\[
J(\phi\psi)=J(\psi)J(\phi).
\]
Hence
\[
\phi\longmapsto
J(\phi^{-1})\big|_{x=y=z=-1}
\]
is a homomorphism to \(\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb Z)\).

The evaluated matrices fix \((1,1,1)^t\), so they act on the quotient by that primitive vector. Projectivizing this rank-two action gives a homomorphism
\[
\rho:\operatorname{IA}_3\longrightarrow H,
\]
where
\[
H=\langle A,B,C\rangle,\qquad
A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
B=\begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
C=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}
\]
are regarded in \(\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb Z)\).

For completeness, the entire evaluated image lies in \(H\): its matrices are congruent to the identity modulo two, and the even Euclidean algorithm shows that the projective level-two subgroup is generated by \(A,B,C\). Indeed \(BA\) and \(CA\), projectively, perform the elementary operations adding twice one coordinate to the other. For an odd-even primitive column these operations strictly reduce the larger absolute value until the column is \((\pm1,0)^t\).

Direct Fox differentiation gives
\[
\rho(a)=B,\qquad
\rho(b)=A,\qquad
\rho(m)=AB,\qquad
\rho(d)=C,\qquad
\rho(e)=AC.
\tag{4}
\]

Moreover,
\[
H\cong C_2*C_2*C_2.
\tag{5}
\]
An elementary ping-pong proof uses their actions
\[
A(t)=-t,\qquad B(t)=2-t,\qquad C(t)=\frac{t}{2t-1}
\]
and the disjoint domains
\[
(-\infty,0),\qquad(1,\infty),\qquad(0,1).
\]
Each involution sends the other two domains into its own.

Now let
\[
R=\mathbb F_2\langle\!\langle \alpha,\beta,\chi\rangle\!\rangle/
(\alpha^2,\beta^2,\chi^2),
\]

\[
A\mapsto1+\alpha,\qquad B\mapsto1+\beta,\qquad C\mapsto1+\chi
\]
define a homomorphism \(H\to R^\times\). The filtered-unit commutator identity gives
\[
\gamma_4(H)\longmapsto 1+I^4.
\tag{6}
\]

\[
a:\beta,\quad b:\alpha,\quad

In characteristic two this simplifies to
\[

1+\alpha\chi\beta+\chi\alpha\beta

\tag{7}

u\notin\gamma_4(\operatorname{IA}_3).

The Fox homomorphism maps the reflections \(A,B,C\) into their free product. Map that free product to
\[
U=\operatorname{UT}_4(\mathbb F_2)
\]
by
\[
A\mapsto I+E_{12},\qquad
B\mapsto I+E_{34},\qquad
C\mapsto I+E_{23}.
\]
These assignments are valid because all three matrices are involutions.

The resulting homomorphism
\[
\operatorname{IA}_3\longrightarrow U
\]
sends the explicit 92-letter automorphism \(u\) above to
\[
I+E_{14}\ne I.
\]
This was checked by multiplying the literal target word, independently of the derivation calculation.

But \(U\) has nilpotency class three, so every element of
\(\gamma_4(\operatorname{IA}_3)\) maps to the identity. Thus
\[
u\notin\gamma_4(\operatorname{IA}_3).
\]
Together with the exact Jacobi identity and the independently checked integral Magnus calculation,
\[
u\in\gamma_3(\operatorname{IA}_3)\cap\mathcal A_4(3).
\]

Therefore
\[
\boxed{(3,3)\in\mathcal D,}
\]
whereas the prescribed answer excludes this pair. The claimed classification cannot be proved with the definitions as written; an indexing convention or another hypothesis must be corrected.
